body:
Investigated further; the mechanism and scope are sharper than the original report:

**Scope**: any text that is not a complete menhir program — dangling `;`, trailing operator, body-less `let … in` chains — takes FastParse's append-a-hole retry, and `strip_appended_hole` then leaves the loaded zipper holding an ill-formed top-level segment: a final infix/prefix operator with no operand and no grout (the typing parser would have regrouted). The program text itself round-trips fine.

**Loss point**: at print, trigger re-emission (`Triggers.refractor_seg_to_seg_with`) computes `Segment.skel` per segment level. On the ill-formed top level, skel raises `Failure("Skel.push_output: split_kids: index out of bounds")` (not even the documented `Nonconvex_segment`) and the catch-all silently abandons wrapping for that level. Emission recurses per tile child, so **invocations targeting terms nested inside any tile child (let defs, parens, fn bodies) survive; only invocations on top-level terms are dropped**. That is why binding-chain fragments usually look fine — their content sits in def children — while `^^probe(f(1));\n^^probe(f(2));` loses both.

**Also affected**: `^^probe(1 + 1);\nlet a = 2 in` and `let a = 2 in\n^^probe(a + 1);\nlet b = 3 in` both drop the top-level invocation — so the body-less-let case is real, just masked when targets are nested.

**Fix directions** (a design call): (a) emission-side — heal the segment for skel purposes only, e.g. append a temporary convex grout before computing skel and drop it from the emitted result (the missing final operand is the only ill-formedness these loads produce), keeping text byte-fidelity; (b) load-side — keep the appended hole as Grout (matching the typing parser and paste, cf. 49dbc8063f), at the cost of the text round-trip gaining a trailing `¿`. The silent catch-all in `refractor_seg_to_seg_with` deserves at least a console note either way.
